comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @eiriktsarpalis, @layomia See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/51302 proposes adding `DateOnly` and `TimeOnly` support to System.Text.Json: on the serializer, reader, writer, and DOM types. We'll not get to all of this in 6.0 but can support them at `JsonSerializer` level now, using internal converters and building on ISO 8601 support. FYI @devsko, @mattjohnsonpint, @eiriktsarpalis, @steveharter, @tarekgh, @ericstj.
Author: layomia
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Text.Json`
Milestone: 6.0.0
@layomia can you move the needed part of the proposal here and we can proceed with that?
@tarekgh 👍 . I added some notes in the description.

I believe that supporting the `DateOnly` and `TimeOnly` types at the `JsonSerializer` level alone will cover most usage scenarios for users that want this support in System.Text.Json for .NET 6.0. I'm proposing that we scope it this way given other STJ work for this release. We could consider more support from https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/51302 given more user feedback, but for now I think we can address the rest in .NET 7/future.
Sounds good to me.  Is this ready for API review?  Should it be marked to get it on the backlog?
We're intentionally only doing the internal converters in this iteration, so no new APIs will be added at this stage.
This should probably be done in conjunction with #29932 (implementation PR #51492) since they're largely related work.

I thought @layomia's API suggestion was needed to expose the converter to the source generator?  Could be wrong.
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/b1e20bf4b72999ba2241dfe0590e5a8f06533a4e/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/ref/System.Text.Json.cs#L873-L897

@ericstj @eiriktsarpalis yup the source generator would need these APIs. No harm in getting this API approved and getting generator support implemented at the same time as the non-source gen code-paths.

Surely, for netstandard 2.0 targeted library it would not be possible to even reference types that need those converters as something to create serializers for. The source generator would never reference a converter for a type not seen in the object hierarchy, as that would defeat being trimer friendly.

I suppose it might be possible for a user created .netstandard2.0 library (that uses the generator for serialization and will ultimately be used in a .net6+ app) to reference another package that is multitargeted which adds some properties of these types for a .net6+ build, but generally those properties would not be serialization critical, since they totally won’t exist on older runtimes. So this normally won’t make a difference. In the rare case it does, the netstandard2.0 user library using source generators could multitarget, and would then have the extra properties in the .net6+ version(s). 

That is kind of fundamental though. Any shape change only seen in a multitargeted version of a referenced package will never be included in a .netstandard2.0 single-targeted library’s source generated serializers, since to do otherwise would require reflection, and avoiding that reflection is basically the whole point of the source generator.

It might be nice to have some form of diagnostic warning for the library author if any such omited properties are detected, and thus won’t be included in the generated serializers. However, I’m not sure that is something that is even feasible for an analyzer, as it requires knowledge of the tfm graph, and knowing what is contained in the binaries of the other targeted tfms. In any case that would be a topic for a different issue.

> These APIs would be in net6.0 only, correct? IOW, the JSON source generator would gracefully do something sane when targeting netstandard2.0 where these don't exist, correct?

STJ builds for .NET Core, Framework, and Standard. The API shape is consistent across the TFMs. It is valid for a project targeting .NET Standard to use the generator so long as there's a reference to STJ.dll. The generator only runs if the `[JsonSerializable]` attribute is used in the user code. We can assume that if the attribute is present, STJ is also present and we can generate code that references source-gen APIs.

> It might be nice to have some form of diagnostic warning for the library author if any such omited properties are detected, and thus won’t be included in the generated serializers. However, I’m not sure that is something that is even feasible for an analyzer, as it requires knowledge of the tfm graph, and knowing what is contained in the binaries of the other targeted tfms. In any case that would be a topic for a different issue.

I'm not sure what can be done regarding this specific issue.

Related issues might arise when stale metadata is passed to the serializer to represent a given type. Actionable mitigations for right now are to include a versioning mechanism in the generated code so that the serializer can reject state implementations at runtime. This work is part of https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/45448. Also we'd encourage users to always (re-)run the generator when building rather than generate once and save the output. This would reduce chances of having stale/mismatched generated code.

In general we do want to provide diagnostics & additional tooling if they can prevent issues, where possible, as the situations arise.

> STJ builds for .NET Core, Framework, and Standard. The API shape is consistent across the TFMs. It is valid for a project targeting .NET Standard to use the generator so long as there's a reference to STJ.dll. The generator only runs if the `[JsonSerializable]` attribute is used in the user code. We can assume that if the attribute is present, STJ is also present and we can generate code that references source-gen APIs.

Sounds good. I just want to make sure we don't accidentally generate code that doesn't work in .NET Standard 2.0 anymore. @KevinCathcart's comment makes sense but we need to keep in mind that people sometimes copy types and make them internal in their project. Not sure it's worth hardening the generator for this, but we know that some people do that.

If somebody did add an internal copy of System.DateOnly to their downlevel library, what would the options even be? 

One (not ideal) option is that the Source Generator tries to use the built-in converter, and fails with a compile error, because it is not present. Option 2 is that the source generator sees the built-in converter does not exist, and generates it own error. Option 3 would be is that in the absence of the built-in converter it generates code treating it like any other user defined type.

Options 2 or 3 are nicer than option one. Both look at a quick glance like they should not be hard to implement. Number 3 would presumably be incompatible with .net6’s serialization by default, but I think the user could register a custom converter for the type to make it compatible. Number 2 would not allow for that possibility, but avoids incompatible serialization if the user provided nothing custom.

One last last possible option would be to emit a compatible version of the converter into the generated code. (Yeah, A decent extra chunk of code, and generally a bad idea, especially for an uncommon edge case. I only mention it for completeness.)

There may be other reasonable options, but none spring to mind.

The `DateOnly` and `TimeOnly` types are not present in .NET Standard/Framework which presents a challenge with the implementation of their support in System.Text.Json, in both the source-gen and non-source-gen cases.

In the non-source-gen case, the types are present in .NET 6.0 or greater, but not .NET Framework. If we support them in the dynamic serializer implementation, we would need to either support them only in .NET 6.0/higher (throwing `NotSupportedException` otherwise). This could cause confusion about what is supported across the TFMs we build for.

In the source-gen case, we can't simply add `JsonConverter<T>`-returning properties representing these types to the [`JsonMetadataServices` APIs](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/e0024e22c7761cbbdd10a845f8b0269ea654cbfc/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/ref/System.Text.Json.cs#L910-L936), since they are only present in .NET 6.0/higher. We have the option of bifurcating the API ref for System.Text.Json and only including these APIs in .NET 6.0/higher, but we haven't done this yet for `System.Text.Json` and it doesn't buy us much since we'd still need to throw `NotSupportedException` for non-NET 6.0 cases under the covers.

It seems that a good solution would be to ship these new types in a new .NET Standard 2.0 assembly, and then support them across all the TFMs given the supplementary OOB implementations. It's too late to do this for .NET 6.0, so the proposal is to:

- [ ] Explicitly throw `NotSupportedException` when (de)serializing `Date/TimeOnly` types, both in source-gen and non-source-gen cases
- [ ] Provide custom converter samples for these types in our [JSON documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json-overview?pivots=dotnet-5-0) as a workaround for cases where the types are available (cc @tdykstra)
- [ ] Consider built-in support for the types in .NET 7, likely based on shipping an OOB .NET Standard 2.0 assembly containing the types

The tasks for this issue are the first two items on this checklist, after which the issue would be closed and re-absorbed into https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/51302 which will include work for the last bullet.

cc @steveharter, @eiriktsarpalis, @tarekgh, @ericstj, @terrajobst
What might be a good name for a netstandard2.0 package containing DateOnly/TimeOnly?
Hmm difficult to say. Maybe we need two assemblies `System.DateOnly` and `System.TimeOnly`.

> Consider built-in support for the types in .NET 7, likely based on shipping an OOB .NET Standard 2.0 assembly containing the types

IMHO we'll have types added over time that will not be present in `netstandard2.0` and not OOBed.  Do we really think that any type that is natively supported in the JSON serializer has to be available on all frameworks?  We should definitely decide if the types are officially OOB'ed and support them in both their inbox and OOB'ed locations, but OOBing shouldn't be a requirement.
I second @ericstj here. Just to be clear there is no plans to have OOB for DateOnly and TimeOnly and I don't think we should have it.

I don't think that every type that is natively supported in the serializer has to be available on all frameworks. We're giving special consideration to the `Date/TimeOnly` types since we anticipate that they'll be popular and used extensively with System.Text.Json. My angle with the proposal above was to have consistent support within STJ for these popular types.

> Just to be clear there is no plans to have OOB for DateOnly and TimeOnly and I don't think we should have it.

Is it something we could consider? Why do you think we shouldn't have it?

Alternative plans would be to (these would also apply to other types not in .NET Standard):

- Support the types statically in STJ for .NET 6.0/greater and support other TFMs with reflection (not agreeable with the JSON source gen design)
- Support the types statically in STJ for .NET 6.0/greater and throw `NotSupportedException` for other TFMs

Are there others that come to mind?

> Alternative plans would be to (these would also apply to other types not in .NET Standard):

Assuming we're never planning on shipping a given set of types as a netstandard nuget package then probably just throwing `NotSupportedException` in older TFMs should be fine.

At the moment it's not in the plans too OOB it.  If that changes we deal with it at that time.  JSON could add the converters along with it should we OOB.

>  just throwing NotSupportedException in older TFMs should be fine

Assuming you're talking about runtime?  What if we just "don't care" on old TFMs.  If someone wants to go out of their way to backport a type and use it, they get what they get.  They could also port the converter and apply it to the type if they want to.

On new frameworks with the type, we expose the converter and source gen uses it.  When source gen finds one of these "special" types it can do a lookup to see if the converter (as exposed in STJ) exists, if it doesn't than we could just handle the type as is (perhaps emit a warning if we are *really* certain we identified the type correctly).  Presumably this isn't all that different from other types that STJ knows about, or perhaps source gen often just "assumes" that the built in converter is present?

For types that we don't know about, we treat them as objects with properties and fields. That policy has largely worked out okay these past few releases. This is almost certainly the current behavior for the `Date/TimeOnly` types today, for both source-gen and non-source gen cases.

I do propose changing the treat-as-object behavior for these (potentially popular) types in .NET 6.0 (to `NotSupportedException` being thrown) so that we can avoid breaking change considerations like we had for the new [`TimeSpan` support](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/29932), when we land on the right approach in 7.0. However, by just logging a warning and proceeding with object semantics, we could be justified in changing the behavior in the future since there was some form of notice. This would only be viable in source-gen scenarios though, and throwing `NSE` across the board would be consistent.

We discussed this during API review, and came to the conclusion that the source generator should bind to `DateOnly` and `TimeOnly` so long as a type matching the full name has been found. So any well-typed POCO containing `System.DateOnly` or `System.TimeOnly` members would trigger source generation regardless of whether the runtime contains the designated types or its converter definitions.

We could try going the extra mile, detecting whether the found `System.DateTime` is the "real" type, but concensus in API review was that we didn't particularly care about that corner case. In any case we use identical semantics for optionally present types: for example, an application that uses a custom `System.Guid` type (with the framework instance being trimmed) would also result in the source generator being invoked for the custom type.
